question: Can a Scrum project still have a project manager?
options: No, the Scrum Master replaces the project manager, so the role does not exist in any Scrum project
Yes, and the project manager assigns the Scrum team's daily tasks and approves each user story
No, because Scrum teams are not part of a larger project and so have no need for project management
Yes, the overall project can still have one, but they do not tell the Scrum team what to do

question: A developer says at the daily scrum that they are blocked. What is the best response from the team and Scrum Master?
options: The team can suggest who might help, and the Scrum Master helps remove the impediment
The blocker is logged and discussed at the next sprint review, once the stakeholders are present
The sprint is extended by the number of days the developer was blocked, so the work can be finished
The Scrum Master orders another developer to take over the task and the blocked person moves on

question: A team is new to Scrum. What might be needed?
options: More coaching and training on how Scrum works, from the Scrum Master or from others brought in
A project manager to run the daily scrum for them until they are comfortable with the framework
A longer sprint so that they can avoid holding the ceremonies while they learn the framework
Fewer ceremonies until the product owner is happy that the team understands the framework

question: Who typically chairs the daily scrum, going round the team and asking each person where they are at?
options: The Scrum Master
The product owner
A stakeholder invited by the product owner
The project manager

question: Which description of the development team is correct?
options: Multidisciplinary, self-organising, and decides what work will be done and who will do what
A group directed by the product owner, who assigns each person's tasks
A group of developers only, with testers working separately
Specialists who each only work within their own role, directed by the Scrum Master

question: What does 'cross-functional' mean for a Scrum team?
options: The team is made up of people borrowed from different departments, each with their own line manager
Every member performs every role at the same time
Each member only works on tasks matching their job title
No one has a predefined role; everyone chips in on a task even if it is not their usual type of work

question: A Scrum team has a developer from sales and a DevOps engineer from marketing, each answering to their own line managers. What does the training say?
options: This is fine as long as the Scrum Master approves it and the line managers are kept informed
This is not how it should work; it complicates things and stops the team focusing on its sprint backlog
This is encouraged, because it spreads knowledge and good practice across the departments
This is only acceptable for DevOps engineers, because they work across departments anyway

question: What does 'co-located' mean for a Scrum team?
options: Only the product owner and the Scrum Master need to be together, so they can coach the others
The team must share a physical office so that the daily scrum can happen face to face in person
The team must be in the same time zone and the same building, as well as using the same board
Not necessarily physically together, but with virtual ways to communicate, such as messaging and a virtual board

question: Who is accountable for the development team's productivity?
options: Only the product owner
Only the Scrum Master
Everyone on the team
The project manager

question: You are the DevOps engineer on a Scrum team, and a task needs doing that is not directly DevOps. What should you do?
options: Decline it, because it is not a DevOps task and should go to a developer on the team instead
Wait for the Scrum Master to assign it to a developer who has the right job title for it
Do whatever is required if you have the capacity, perhaps with someone alongside you to help
Pass it back to the product owner, so the story can be re-prioritised for a different team

question: What does it mean that the Scrum team is 'self-organising, accountable and empowered'?
options: The Scrum Master assigns each task and the team then confirms the assignments
People outside the team need to trust it and let it get on with its work
A manager approves each task before it starts, to make sure it is accountable
Stakeholders direct the team's work every day, through the daily scrum

question: What is an artifact in Scrum?
options: One of the three pillars of Scrum
A tangible thing that is produced and represents work
A role with specific responsibilities in the team
A meeting held at a fixed point in the sprint

question: Which list contains ONLY Scrum artifacts?
options: Product backlog, sprint planning, increment
Product backlog, sprint backlog, sprint review
Sprint backlog, daily scrum, increment
Product backlog, sprint backlog, increment

question: Which list contains ONLY Scrum ceremonies (events)?
options: Product backlog, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective
Sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective
Sprint planning, daily scrum, increment, sprint review
Sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint backlog, sprint retrospective

question: Which list contains ONLY Scrum roles?
options: Product owner, project manager, development team
Product owner, Scrum Master, increment
Scrum Master, development team, sprint
Product owner, Scrum Master, development team

question: Which list contains ONLY the three pillars of Scrum?
options: Collaboration, inspection, adaptation
Transparency, inspection, retrospection
Transparency, iteration, adaptation
Transparency, inspection, adaptation

question: How do the product backlog and the sprint backlog relate?
options: The sprint backlog is the ordered list of everything needed; the product backlog is the subset selected for the current sprint
The product backlog is only seen by stakeholders; the sprint backlog is only seen by developers
They are the same list, held in two different tools
The product backlog is the ordered list of everything needed; the sprint backlog is the subset selected for the current sprint

question: What is an increment?
options: A working piece of software built on top of all previous increments, as a stepping stone towards the product goal
The list of bugs that were found during the sprint and that the team will fix in the next one
A single finished feature, considered separately from the rest of the software and the earlier increments
The document describing what the team will do in the next sprint and which stories it will pick up

question: At the end of a sprint, the new login feature works but the rest of the software no longer does. Is this a proper increment?
options: No, an increment must be a working piece of software, not one feature that breaks the rest
Yes, as long as the product owner approves the login feature at the sprint review meeting
No, because increments must always contain at least five user stories to be worth reviewing
Yes, because the sprint goal was only the login feature and nothing else needed to keep working

question: How do the sprint goal and the product goal differ?
options: The product goal summarises the focus of one sprint; the sprint goal is the product wanted at the end of all the sprints
The sprint goal is the list of all user stories; the product goal is the burn down chart
The sprint goal summarises the focus of one sprint; the product goal is the product wanted at the end of all the sprints
They are the same, but one is written by the product owner and the other by the Scrum Master

question: What decides how many sprints the team has to reach the product goal?
options: It is unlimited; Scrum continues until the product backlog is empty, however long that takes
The Scrum Master, who fixes it at ten sprints so the team can plan its work in advance
The time and budget available for allocating people; if the deadline is hard, scope may be reduced
The stakeholders, who extend the sprints until every item on the backlog has been completed

question: On the course task board, which Scrum idea is the 'To do' list most similar to, and which is 'In progress' most similar to?
options: To do is similar to the increment; in progress is similar to the product goal
To do is similar to the product backlog; in progress is similar to the sprint
To do is similar to the sprint; in progress is similar to the product backlog
To do is similar to the sprint review; in progress is similar to the retrospective

question: When does sprint planning happen, and what is its purpose?
options: At the end of each sprint, to demonstrate the working increment to the stakeholders who attend
At the start of each sprint, to define the sprint goal, select backlog items and plan how the work will get done
Every day at the same time, to share progress and raise blockers so the team can help each other
After the sprint review, to reflect on how the team worked together and what to improve next time

question: A sprint is typically about two weeks long. Which statement is correct?
options: It is always one month, so that each increment is large enough to be worth showing to stakeholders
It changes in length from sprint to sprint, to match the amount of work that is on the backlog
It is always exactly two weeks in every team, because that is what the Scrum framework requires
It can vary, and can even be as short as a day, but within a team it is a fixed length

question: Which items does the team pull into the sprint backlog at sprint planning?
options: Every item on the product backlog that has not yet been started, so nothing is left behind
Whichever items the individual developers like the most, so that they stay motivated during the sprint
Items from the top of the prioritised product backlog that the team can realistically get done in the sprint
Items from the bottom of the product backlog, so that the higher priorities are not rushed

question: What are the three standard daily scrum questions?
options: What did you do last week? What are you going to do next week? Do you have any budget issues?
What did you do yesterday? What are you going to do today? Do you have any blockers?
What did you do today? What are you going to do tomorrow? Do you have any blockers?
What did you do yesterday? What are you going to do this sprint? Do you have any risks?

question: Why is it important to listen to everyone at the daily scrum, rather than just saying your own update?
options: The daily scrum is the place the product backlog is re-ordered
The Scrum Master marks you down if you are not paying attention
You might need to help a teammate overcome their blocker
The stakeholders review the updates at the end of the day

question: What is the sprint review?
options: A blameless meeting where the team reflects on its processes and chooses improvements for next time
A meeting at the end of the sprint, sometimes with stakeholders invited, to review the work and demonstrate the increment
A meeting at the start of the sprint where the sprint goal is agreed and the items are selected
A short daily meeting where each person says what they did yesterday and raises any blockers

question: Which statement correctly contrasts the sprint review with the sprint retrospective?
options: The retrospective demonstrates what was done, to stakeholders; the review is the team's reflection on its process and improvements
Both are the team's blameless reflection, but one includes the stakeholders
The review demonstrates what was done, to stakeholders; the retrospective is the team's reflection on its process and improvements
Both are demonstrations of the increment, but one is held daily

question: Why is the sprint retrospective described as blameless?
options: Because the stakeholders attend and the team does not want to admit its mistakes in front of them
It is a reflection on how the team can work better together, not a chance to point fingers
Because the Scrum Master is held responsible for every missed task, so no one else is blamed
Because only the things that went well are discussed, so that no one feels uncomfortable

question: How should the team feel by the end of a sprint retrospective?
options: That they have a few manageable improvements to work on in the next sprint
That nothing needs to change because the sprint is already over
That they have a long list of every possible issue to fix at once
That they have identified who caused each problem

question: At the end of a sprint, some user stories are only partly finished and others were never started. What happens to them?
options: They are deleted, because the sprint has ended and the stakeholders will raise them again later
They automatically roll over into the next sprint backlog so the team can carry on with them
They stay in the sprint backlog until they are done, whichever sprint that ends up being
They go back into the product backlog and are reviewed at the next sprint planning meeting

question: Why do unfinished items not automatically go into the next sprint?
options: Priorities and requirements may have changed since the last sprint planning meeting
Only the Scrum Master is allowed to carry items over, and only with the stakeholders' approval
Unfinished items must be rewritten from scratch by the stakeholders before they can be reused
The sprint backlog can only contain brand-new items that have never been started by the team

question: Which sequence of events within and around a sprint is correct?
options: Sprint planning, daily scrums during the sprint, sprint retrospective, sprint review
Sprint planning, sprint review, daily scrums during the sprint, sprint retrospective
Sprint planning, daily scrums during the sprint, sprint review, sprint retrospective
Sprint review, sprint planning, daily scrums during the sprint, sprint retrospective

question: Which of these is part of the development work on a user story?
options: Chairing the retrospective, choosing the improvements and recording the action items for next time
Re-ordering the product backlog and negotiating priorities with stakeholders for the next sprint
Deciding the sprint goal and the product goal, then agreeing them with the product owner
Code design, unit testing, coding, reviewing code, version control and updating documentation

question: Which user story should a developer pick next from the sprint backlog?
options: Whichever one the Scrum Master assigns them
Whichever one they find easiest
The one the product owner picks during the daily scrum
One from the top, as the backlog is in priority order

question: What happens when a user story meets its definition of done?
options: It is moved to the next sprint, to be tested again by a different developer before it is released
It is left in the sprint backlog until the sprint review, when the stakeholders decide if it is done
It is moved to the relevant column on the task board, and the developer picks the next story
It is returned to the product backlog for the product owner to close once the sprint has ended

question: What can happen at a retrospective board that tracks mood across the sprint, sometimes called 'cliffs and valleys'?
options: People chart how the sprint felt, such as starting happy and dipping when blockers appeared, with sticky notes
The team estimates the effort of each backlog item using numbered cards, then discusses the outliers
The product owner ranks the stakeholders on a power-interest grid to decide who to keep informed
The Scrum Master plots the story points that are still remaining in the sprint on a daily basis

question: What does a retrospective typically end with?
options: A new set of sprint dates, agreed with the product owner and the Scrum Master
A demonstration of the new increment to the stakeholders who attended the review
A re-ordered product backlog, reflecting the new priorities agreed with the stakeholders
A few manageable action items for improving the next sprint

question: A team lead says that when things go wrong in the team, they should accept responsibility for the whole team. Which Scrum idea is this closest to?
options: Servant leadership of the product owner, who is answerable to the stakeholders for the whole team
A blameless culture, where the focus is on avoiding the problem next time rather than who is at fault
The sprint review, where leaders demonstrate the increment and take the stakeholders' questions
Transparency, where the leader reports each person's failures to the stakeholders in full

question: Which statement defines transparency, the first pillar of Scrum?
options: Stakeholders can see the code as it is written
Everyone presents the facts as they are, with no hidden agenda
The team continuously improves based on what it realises
Anyone on the Scrum team can check the product, process, people and practices

question: Which statement defines inspection?
options: Anyone on the Scrum team can check the product, process, people and practices, rather than a separate inspector
Everyone presents the facts as they are, with no hidden agenda, in front of the rest of the team
The team continuously improves its product and processes based on what it realises along the way
A dedicated inspector reviews the team's work at the end of each sprint and reports to the product owner

question: Which statement defines adaptation?
options: Anyone on the Scrum team can check the product, process, people and practices, not just an inspector
Changing the sprint length every time that the requirements change during the project
Everyone presents the facts as they are, with no hidden agenda, in front of the rest of the team
Continuous improvement based on what the team realises about the product, processes, people and practices

question: A developer admits at the daily scrum that a story is behind schedule, rather than hiding it. Which pillar does this show?
options: Adaptation
Inspection
Transparency
Estimation

question: After a retrospective, the team changes how it runs its daily scrum to make it more useful. Which pillar does this show?
options: Adaptation
Transparency
Prioritisation
Inspection

question: A product manager from outside the Scrum team arrives and criticises how the team works. Why does this not match the inspection pillar?
options: Inspection can only be done by the Scrum Master, who then reports to the rest of the team
Inspection can only be done by stakeholders, and only at the sprint review at the end of the sprint
Inspection is only applied to the code and the product, never to the team's processes or people
Inspection is done by the Scrum team members themselves, not by someone coming in from outside

question: Which statement about a sprint is correct?
options: Scope can never be discussed with the product owner once it has started
Quality can be reduced to hit the sprint goal if the Scrum Master agrees
It has a fixed length and always works towards the product goal
Its length changes from week to week depending on the workload

question: During a sprint, the team learns more about a user story. What can happen to its scope?
options: The Scrum Master decides the new scope alone and tells the developers what has changed
It may be clarified and renegotiated with the product owner, but the team keeps working on the sprint backlog
It can never be discussed with anyone until the sprint review, when the stakeholders are present
The team swaps it for a different story straight away, without checking with the product owner

question: Can the product backlog be changed while a sprint is in progress?
options: No, only the sprint backlog can change during a sprint, and then only by the developers
No, the product backlog is frozen until the sprint review, to protect the sprint goal
Yes, it can be refined as needed, such as adding or adjusting stories as the team learns more
Yes, but only by the Scrum Master, who then tells the product owner what was changed

question: Halfway through a sprint, a developer suggests skipping the performance work to finish on time. What does the sprint rule say?
options: That is allowed if the stakeholders agree at the review
That is allowed because delivering on time matters more than quality
That is allowed if the Scrum Master documents it
Quality does not decrease; changes must not endanger the sprint goal
